title: Quantum computers outperform classical ones, with results you can trust
gist: IBM added three new entries to its quantum advantage tracker in which the novelty is verification, not speed: each uses a different error-handling scheme—Qedma error mitigation cross-checked on Quantinuum hardware, T-gate circuits with built-in error detection from the University of Chicago collaboration, and Algorithmiq's noise-injection calibration—to bound the trustworthiness of results that classical computers cannot check. None of the algorithms are useful yet.

themes.theme: Verification is now the binding constraint on quantum advantage

insights.claim: The central problem is that any result genuinely out of reach of classical computers is also a result classical computers cannot verify, while today's error-prone quantum hardware makes wrong answers a live possibility.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The credibility bottleneck, not raw performance, is what gates commercial adoption of quantum results—verification tooling is the underrated layer.
insights.locator: That’s a more difficult question than it may first appear

insights.claim: IBM's Jay Gambetta drew the line explicitly: trusted computing only matters in the regime where classical simulation is impossible.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for evaluating future quantum claims—demand both classical intractability and an independent trust argument, or discount the claim.
insights.quote: Trusted computing when you can’t do classical simulations is a big deal.
insights.locator: These issues inspired IBM to launch a quantum advantage tracker

insights.claim: Many prior quantum advantage claims have been eroded because algorithm developers built optimized classical algorithms that brought conventional computers back to par.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Quantum advantage is a moving target set by classical algorithm progress—assume any announced advantage has a meaningful probability of being reversed.

insights.claim: The standard workaround—running simplified small-qubit versions, verifying classically, and assuming the algorithm still works at larger scale—is an assumption rather than a proof.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Exposes the epistemic gap in nearly all published quantum results; the three new papers exist specifically to close it.
insights.locator: These issues are typically handled by performing simplified calculations

insights.claim: No one has yet identified a hard-to-compute, easy-to-verify calculation—the factoring-style asymmetry—that today's hardware can actually run.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The cleanest possible proof of quantum advantage remains unavailable, which is why the field is reduced to creative error-handling workarounds.
insights.locator: Unfortunately, if anyone has identified a calculation

themes.theme: Approach one: error mitigation cross-checked across vendors

insights.claim: IBM, RIKEN, and error-mitigation software company Qedma modeled a Floquet process on an Ising model and found that two different classical algorithms run on the Fugaku supercomputer diverged from each other, with one showing net magnetism increasing and the other decreasing.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Classical methods disagreeing with each other is itself the evidence of classical intractability—a cleverer proof structure than a pure timing comparison.
insights.locator: One of the new efforts was a collaboration among IBM

insights.claim: Run on an IBM quantum processor with Qedma's error-mitigation software, the algorithm produced a gradual decrease in magnetism with periodic oscillations—behavior neither classical approximation captured correctly.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Error-mitigation software is doing load-bearing work in the advantage claim, which makes independent mitigation vendors strategically important, not peripheral.
insights.locator: When run on an IBM quantum processor with Qedma’s error-mitigation software

insights.claim: To rule out a consistent hardware-specific error, the team reproduced the result on a Quantinuum processor, using a rival vendor's machine as the control.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Cross-vendor replication is emerging as the de facto trust protocol in quantum—raises the value of a diverse hardware ecosystem rather than a single winner.
insights.locator: To demonstrate that this wasn’t the product of some consistent error

insights.claim: The team identified a flaw in at least one of the classical algorithms: to boost performance it truncates terms that are needed to produce the oscillatory behavior.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Shows classical baselines can be quietly wrong rather than merely slow—an argument that quantum advantage may be understated in some comparisons.
insights.locator: They also identified a problem in at least one

themes.theme: Approach two: complexity guarantees plus built-in error detection

insights.claim: An IBM and University of Chicago collaboration built circuits mostly from easily simulable Clifford gates but sprinkled in a few non-Clifford T gates chosen because Z rotations are implemented by virtual frame tracking and add no extra noise on IBM hardware.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Exploiting a hardware quirk where certain gates are noise-free is the kind of co-design edge that is hard for competitors to copy across architectures.
insights.quote: Z rotations (including T gates) are special in our hardware: they are implemented by virtual frame tracking and do not add extra noise

insights.claim: Gambetta argues the T gates give the result a stronger complexity argument because such circuits can be proven on average to be exponentially hard for classical computers to sample.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A provable average-case hardness argument is the durable defense against classical algorithms catching up—the key differentiator versus earlier advantage claims.
insights.quote: It’s got a stronger complexity argument because of the [T gates], which you can prove on average is exponentially hard to sample for a classical computer,
insights.locator: But the T gates also help ensure

insights.claim: The design links extra qubits around the algorithm's periphery so gentle mid-circuit measurements can detect errors and discard affected runs, at the cost of also throwing out valid results flagged by erroneous reads.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Post-selection buys fidelity by burning throughput—an efficiency tax that must be counted when comparing quantum and classical run costs.
insights.locator: The work also linked in a few additional qubits

themes.theme: Approach three: bounding residual noise by injecting it

insights.claim: Quantum software developer Algorithmiq used an algorithm similar to Google's 'quantum echoes' work, where a forward process is reversed imperfectly so noise creates an echo that classical simulation can only approximate—with different simplifications yielding different answers.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Independent software firms, not just hardware makers, are generating the advantage claims—the quantum value chain is bifurcating.
insights.locator: The last of the new results comes from quantum software developer Algorithmiq

insights.claim: Algorithmiq selected the lowest-noise region of the processor, used neighboring qubits as error sentinels, optimized control signals, then intentionally injected noise to measure its effect and extrapolate back to a bounded residual noise estimate.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Deliberate noise injection to calibrate an upper bound is a transferable technique—likely to become standard practice regardless of which hardware wins.
insights.locator: The people behind the manuscript set to work removing all the noise

insights.claim: The team repeated the entire procedure on a separate IBM processor with a different noise pattern, allowing them to state a calculable ceiling on the error rate of their result.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A stated, calculable error bound is what turns a quantum output into something a scientist or engineer could actually rely on.
insights.locator: They also repeated the entire process on a separate IBM processor

themes.theme: The honest read on what this is worth

insights.claim: None of the three algorithms are useful in any real sense—even those modeling quantum systems use incredibly simplified models that reflect no real-world system.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Explicit no-commercial-value disclosure from a sympathetic science editor is the correct anchor against vendor announcement enthusiasm.
insights.quote: Cynically, it’s definitely the case that none of these algorithms are useful in any real sense.

insights.claim: This entire class of work—computing directly on noisy hardware qubits—will fade within a few years once reasonable numbers of error-corrected qubits arrive, and some companies are already withholding public hardware access until then.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A named expiry date on the NISQ era implies limited durable value in noisy-hardware business models—favor firms whose roadmaps target error correction.

insights.claim: The lasting value is in the transferable techniques—minimizing noise, understanding its nature, identifying what makes it worse—which should improve performance on error-corrected hardware too.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Noise characterization IP survives the modality transition, making error-software companies a less binary bet than hardware vendors.
insights.locator: The less cynical take is that the hardware is out there

insights.claim: Gambetta frames the field as having moved from comparing real materials in a regime where classical methods still work, to toy models in a regime where classical methods fail but the quantum result can be trusted—with the holy grail being a trusted comparison against a real material or experiment.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit three-stage maturity ladder—use it to grade every future quantum announcement and to time when the technology becomes commercially relevant.
insights.quote: The holy grail is to compare a real material or a real experiment to a quantum computer,
